claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature BCC phase.
Chemical short-range order developing during cooling is the primary driver of transformation from BCC to a multiphase microstructure.
The proposed short-range-order clusters preferentially segregate Cr and Al from the other elements.
Cr- and Al-associated short-range-order clusters lower the local free energy.
These short-range-order clusters lower the nucleation barrier for ordered secondary phases.
Short-range order can trigger nucleation and growth of B2 or sigma phases during slow cooling or moderate-temperature annealing.
Differences in atomic size and mixing enthalpy among Cr, Al, and the other transition metals promote local short-range order during slow cooling.
Atomic diffusion is sufficiently active for the proposed mechanism around 600–800 °C.
At very low temperatures, atomic mobility is too limited for the proposed short-range ordering and subsequent phase formation.
Extremely rapid quenching suppresses the evolution of short-range order and subsequent ordering.
Slow cooling and/or intermediate-temperature annealing will increase the fraction of ordered secondary phases relative to rapid quenching.
A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 sample will predominantly retain metastable BCC with minimal secondary ordered phases.
The identity and volume fractions of the ordered phases are sensitive to slight compositional variations and thermal-processing history.
After identical annealing at approximately 700 °C, the slowly cooled material should retain a statistically significant excess of ordered-phase fraction or size over the initially quenched material.

contradictions.description: The mechanism is said to operate during 600–800 °C annealing, but both comparison groups are subsequently annealed at about 700 °C. Thus, similar ordering in the initially quenched group could result from SRO forming during that anneal and would not necessarily falsify the mechanism. This also changes the stated unannealed rapid-quench baseline.
